input.add_to_description: Day 8: Maud and Wren will leave for Stonebridge only after the Ford Chapel barrow is sealed (their road runs south, away from the chapel, but Maud wants to see it done first). Wren is not allowed at the sealing; Corwin said she may bring the lamp.

entries.text: notebook: updated Wren

Your answer first: Maud has settled it. Stonebridge is south and the chapel is north, so the barrow is not on their road. She says she won't leave a stirring thing at her back door with her girl on the cart. She and Wren will wait until it's sealed, and go the same day if all is well. Wren hears this with her mouth shut and her eyes very bright.

You spend the evening as you said. Tessa's breaths come easy against Ilsa's shoulder, a slow sixty by the window, with no rattle in them at all. Osric's arm has closed clean along the split, and he flexes the fingers and says it itches, which is a good sign. Corwin has laid out the ropes and the crowbar by the cart. Tobias's mule is bedded down with an extra feed.

You sleep in the chapel with the broom leaned against the altar, and Wren's sweeping fades off somewhere before you do. You wake at ten to five on Day 9, in the dark, with the frost on the window and the smell of baking from a house nearby. Your hit points are full at 17, all three 1st-level slots are back, and Channel Divinity is ready. Your prayers are as you left them, and you may change the list now.

Outside, the cart is waiting with the mule in harness, the crowbar in the straw, and a heap of sacks that smell of lamp oil. Corwin, Osric, Tobias, Fenn and two more dyers stand round it in the dark with lanterns, stamping to keep warm. Wren is on the chapel step with a lit lamp in both hands. She says nothing at all and holds it out to you.

You are 100 XP short of level 3. The ford is two hours up the road, and the slab lies a hand's width open.

entries.text: notebook: updated Marta Quill

You unbar the door and step into the doorway with the mace in your left hand, the shield on your arm, and the hood of the lantern cracked a finger's width. Your voice is low and even. "Over here, goodwife. The door's open. I'm Brannoc, a healer. Come to the fire, and don't try to talk yet."

She stops at the edge of the lantern's light, swaying. She is about thirty, thin, her hair stuck to her face, her shawl soaked to the knees with fen-water. You check her before she comes in, as you promised. Medicine (25, a natural 20): the picture comes clear at once.

She casts a long, ordinary shadow behind her, pooled by the lantern she carries. Her lips are dry and cracked and a little blue at the corners from chill, with no frost-burn and no gray marks. Her eyes are yellowed at the edges and glassy with fever, but they track you. Her breath smokes in the cold air, and she shivers like a living thing. She is sick and she is alive.

Because your hand is steady and your eye is good, you notice more. Round her wrists and shins is a scatter of old, shallow cuts, the kind a reed-cutter gets from the sharp leaf-edges, and each one is rimmed with a thin pale-green line, as if the skin there were dyed with weak woad. Where the cuts are oldest the line has crept a finger's length up the flesh, spreading like frost on a pane. The sickness is not a cold, and not a chest-fever. It enters through the cuts. That is how it began, and how it spreads. You've never seen the like, but you know where to start. A cut washed clean early, in boiled water and honey, might stop the line. And Lesser Restoration would end the disease in anyone it has already taken.

She reaches the threshold, and her knees go. You catch her. "Marta Quill," she whispers. "From Reedholm. My boy Dab... I was going to Stonebridge... for a healer."

It's half past ten on Day 11. She is in your arms, shaking. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, a fire, and honey, linen, willow-bark and water.

You unbar the door and step into the frame with your mace in your left hand, the shield on your arm, and the lantern hood cracked open a hand's width. The light falls yellow across the causeway. "Over here, goodwife, the door's open. I'm Brannoc, a healer. Come to the fire and sit, and don't try to talk yet."

She stops ten paces off, swaying, and lifts her failing lantern to look at you. You use the minute she takes to look at her, as you promised yourself.

Medicine (25, a natural 20): she is a small, rawboned woman of about thirty in a patched shawl, with reed-cutter's hands and cracked knuckles. She casts a shadow, a thin one, long across the planks in your lantern's glow. Her lips are cracked and dry, and not blue. There is no frost-burn on her skin, no gray marks, nothing of the grave about her. Her eyes are glassy and bright and her cheeks are flushed hot, with the fine shiver of a high fever running through her. She walks like someone sick, not like something dead. She is only a woman who has walked two nights.

And the great clarity of that look gives you more. This isn't a plague that spreads from person to person. The pattern is all wrong for that, and the shape of her sickness, a gut-fever with a cough, is the shape of a water-sickness. In her apron pocket you can see the stoppered neck of a tiny glass phial with a pale green-white scum inside. When she sees you look, she whispers, "From the stems. Where the lights are. I scraped it." Whatever she knows, she has put it together herself. Every case, she says between coughs, drank or washed at the sluice-pool, which is fed from the reeds around the drowned barrow. It is a hard fever and the pool is the source.

You get her to the fire. She sits like a puppet with its strings cut and says her name is Marta Quill and her boy Dab is with her sister, and she was going to Stonebridge for a healer and has gone two nights without sleeping. Her skin is hot and dry. She will not be well without help.

It's a quarter to eleven on Day 11. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, and willow-bark. Lesser Restoration would end her disease outright, and you've two such slots to spend today. You haven't rested since seven this morning.

What does Brannoc do?

sheet.name: Brannoc Ashdown
sheet.opening: Brannoc Ashdown, a young human cleric of the Life domain, has been on the road only a few weeks, walking out from Millbrook Landing, the little river town of fishermen and reed-cutters where he grew up. He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He keeps a promise to carry her work to places that have no healer at all. His past (true and not to be contradicted): as a child he sat beside dying neighbors because Edda had too few hands; the night she told him to leave a dying fisherman and rest, he refused, and the man's daughter later thanked him, which is the root of his stubbornness. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). Brannoc has his mace, chain mail, shield, light crossbow, priest's pack, and 15 gp. Give him a clear, immediate call to act, and room to choose between healing, protecting, and investigating.

features: Divine Domain: Choose one domain related to your deity, such as Life. Each domain is detailed at the end of the class description, and each one provides examples of gods associated with it. Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. It also grants you additional ways to use Channel Divinity when you gain that feature at 2nd level, and additional benefits at 6th, 8th, and 17th levels.

Domain Spells: Each domain has a list of spells--its domain spells--that you gain at the cleric levels noted in the domain description. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Channel Divinity (1/rest): At 2nd level, you gain the ability to channel divine energy directly from your deity, using that energy to fuel magical effects. You start with two such effects: Turn Undead and an effect determined by your domain. Some domains grant you additional effects as you advance in levels, as noted in the domain description. When you use your Channel Divinity, you choose which effect to create. You must then finish a short or long rest to use your Channel Divinity again. Some Channel Divinity effects require saving throws. When you use such an effect from this class, the DC equals your cleric spell save DC. Beginning at 6th level, you can use your Channel Divinity twice between rests, and beginning at 18th level, you can use it three times between rests. When you finish a short or long rest, you regain your expended uses.

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead: As an action, you present your holy symbol and speak a prayer censuring the undead. Each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet of you must make a Wisdom saving throw. If the creature fails its saving throw, it is turned for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. A turned creature must spend its turns trying to move as far away from you as it can, and it can't willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It also can't take reactions. For its action, it can use only the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that prevents it from moving. If there's nowhere to move, the creature can use the Dodge action.

Channel Divinity: Preserve Life: Starting at 2nd level, you can use your Channel Divinity to heal the badly injured. As an action, you present your holy symbol and evoke healing energy that can restore a number of hit points equal to five times your cleric level. Choose any creatures within 30 feet of you, and divide those hit points among them. This feature can restore a creature to no more than half of its hit point maximum. You can't use this feature on an undead or a construct. At level 3: 15 hit points to divide.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

You unbar the door, mace in your left hand and shield on your arm, and open the hooded lantern a hand's width. "Over here, goodwife. I'm Brannoc, a healer. Come to the fire and sit, and don't try to talk yet."

She comes the last twenty paces in a stumbling rush. She casts a shadow, a long, wavering one, thrown by her own failing lantern against the hut wall, and there are no frost-burns on her hands or face. Her fingers are cracked and cold and ordinary. She is a woman in her thirties in a patched reed-cutter's coat, soaked to the knees, lips dry and split, her hair plastered with sweat. She steps over the threshold and her knees go. You catch her under the arms and ease her down on the bench by the fire.

Medicine (11), a hair short of what a clear read would need: she is feverish, that much is plain. Her skin is hot and dry, her pulse thin and quick, and her breath rattles on the in-breath. Something in her eyes looks pale or yellow in the lantern light, but the light is bad and you can't swear to it. You cannot yet tell whether this is a fever alone, a bad lung, or something that has settled in the liver. You'd want more light and more time to know.

She grips your sleeve and says between coughs: "Marta Quill. Reedholm. My boy, my Dab, he's four, he's with my sister-in-law, I was going to Stonebridge..." Her eyes go unfocused. "The Wick-fires. They came when we cut the reeds by the old mound. Everyone who cut there is sick."

It's twenty-six past ten on Day 11. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, the willow-bark, and honey. Marta is conscious but weakening, and her breath is wet and loud.
